functions.title: Functions, arguments and return values
functions.brief: A function is a named piece of code. Arguments are the values we give it. A return value is the result we get back. A list holds several values in order.
functions.example: temperature_stats([82, 97], 85) passes a list and one reference value. The function returns a dictionary, not a printed sentence.

records.title: JSON, dictionaries and registered values
records.brief: A dictionary connects keys to values. JSON is text used to send a similar structure between programs. A registered limit describes a reference, not the current temperature.
records.example: {"machine_id":"CONV-3"} is JSON text. json.loads turns it into a Python dictionary. 85 C in the register does not mean the sensor reads 85 C.

sql.title: Tables, queries and time windows
sql.brief: A table stores rows with named columns. SELECT reads chosen rows. A filter narrows the result. Our start time is included and our end time is excluded.
sql.example: A reading at 10:00 belongs in [10:00,10:25); a reading exactly at 10:25 does not. This avoids counting a boundary twice in adjacent windows.

contracts.title: Schemas and validation
contracts.brief: A schema describes the allowed structure of data. Validation checks a particular input against that structure. It does not read the user's mind.
contracts.example: A valid ID for CONV-7 can pass all type checks even when the user asked about CONV-3. Compare the actual arguments with the question.

processes.title: Programs, processes and messages
processes.brief: A process is a running program. Two programs can exchange messages instead of importing each other's functions. Our MCP server runs locally in a separate process.
processes.example: The client starts Python with mcp_server.py, writes protocol messages to its input, and reads replies from its output. No cloud server or GPU is needed.

tasks.title: Query a precise temperature window
tasks.purpose: Keep SQL under application control while allowing the model to supply validated query arguments.
tasks.logic: A query filters rows for one device and time window. Include the start, exclude the end. A successful query can return zero rows.
code_walkthrough: In Review, first explain the actual concept and visual on slide 15; then connect it to code. In Practice, introduce the concept at the exercise. Match filtering, sorting and row limits to the fixed query before transferring to temperature data.
QueryArgs normalizes timezone-aware timestamps and checks start < end and a maximum 24-hour window.
Convert the validated times to epoch seconds. Bind values into the fixed SQL question marks; never concatenate user text into SQL.
mode=ro opens a read-only connection; query_only adds another guard. closing releases the database handle even on failure.
ORDER BY gives chronological order. LIMIT 101 lets us detect more than 100 rows and report RESULT_LIMIT instead of silently truncating.
Turn each returned tuple into a dictionary. count equals len(records); an empty list means no matching records, not a temperature of zero.

review.logic: The model supplies bounded values to a defined lookup. The application keeps control of the query itself.

review.title: Why not just call the Python function?
review.logic: For one small application with a few local functions, direct function calling can be enough. MCP is optional; adding it does not make a model smarter.
review.explanation: Our local tool list is prepared in tool_definitions.py. A second application could reuse that Python package, but another language or process needs an agreed interface. MCP, the Model Context Protocol, standardizes messages for discovering and using capabilities. This can reduce separate connection code across applications. The function still performs the same narrow job.
review.worked_example: Keep the local route when it is the simplest fit. Consider MCP when a tool provider should be independently connected, discovered and reused by compatible applications. These are design benefits, not proof that every project needs MCP.

review.title: Three roles, two different connections
review.logic: Function calling links the model to its application. MCP links an application client to a tool server. They describe different connections in the same workflow.
review.explanation: The Host is the whole assistant application. Its Client speaks MCP to a Server that offers a function. In app.py, routes chooses either a local function or an MCPBackend. async with opens the connection for this block and closes it afterward. DeepSeek receives model API requests; it does not connect directly to the local server. A client can test the server with no model present.
review.worked_example: Student -> host -> DeepSeek proposal -> host validation -> MCP client -> server function -> result -> host -> DeepSeek explanation. On the local route, the middle client/server connection becomes an ordinary function call.

options.C: The parameter schema runs the function as soon as the model reads it.

check.explanation: The model proposes a request. The host checks it and owns the MCP client. The server receives the client request and runs its registered function.

check.hint2: In app.py, the host opens MCPBackend. The model API does not open that local connection.

review.title: Local messages and a deliberately limited environment
review.logic: A process is a running program. Our client starts a separate Python program for the server and exchanges messages through its input and output streams. This transport is called stdio.
review.explanation: server_parameters selects the same Python interpreter and the server script. Its environment allowlist does not intentionally pass DEEPSEEK_API_KEY. The specification reader has no need for that key. This reduces unnecessary credential exposure, but a separate process under the same user is not an automatic file-permission sandbox. Keep stdout for protocol messages and send diagnostic logs to stderr. No HTTP port or GPU is required here.
review.worked_example: The model client needs the DeepSeek key; the local register-reading server does not. These responsibilities can be separated without claiming that MCP itself grants or enforces all permissions.

review.title: Discover a tool before requesting its result
review.logic: A catalogue describes what can be requested. It is not the requested equipment data. Discovering tools does not execute all of them.
review.explanation: Read the lecture client: list_tools asks for names, descriptions and argument schemas. call_tool names one function and supplies an argument dictionary. await means wait for that operation to finish before using its result. The known machine should return a structured record; an unknown machine should produce an explicit error. This independent check separates connection problems from model-selection problems.

options.B: The CONV-3 registered value, because listing a tool also runs it.

check.explanation: Discovery describes an available capability. It does not supply its result. A separate call_tool request carries the chosen tool name and machine_id.

review.logic: The server is an interface around a function we already trust enough to test. Its wrapper should not create a second source of specification data.
review.explanation: MCPServer creates the server object. @server.tool registers the following function; it does not run it immediately. The return annotation dict[str, Any] and structured_output=True request structured output. The alias read_spec refers to the existing reader, avoiding an accidental call back to the wrapper itself. Known business failures become ToolError rather than successful-looking text. Use the lecture implementation to understand the pattern, then complete the seminar wrapper yourself.
review.worked_example: A CONV-3 request reaches read_spec and returns its source and reference value. A nonexistent machine reaches the error path. Both paths tell the client what actually happened.

review.title: Structured results and honest failure signals
review.logic: A string that looks like JSON is still text. A structured result lets the application inspect fields without guessing from a sentence.
review.explanation: unpack_result first checks is_error. If it is true, the course raises a tool failure instead of treating the message as data. Next it requires a structured_content dictionary and validates our ToolResult envelope. status, data, source, version and error are this seminar's field names, not mandatory fields for every MCP server. The lecture uses an ok-based envelope, so do not interchange their keys.
review.worked_example: Connection failure, unsupported protocol/schema, tool failure and an incorrect final model answer are different problems. A correct structured tool result is evidence to check the answer against, not a guarantee that the answer is correct.

options.C: Keep the failure and report that no specification value was confirmed.

check.explanation: unpack_result checks is_error before using data. An error message containing a number is not evidence of a successful tool result. Preserve the failure for diagnosis.
check.hint1: Which field tells the client whether the operation reported a failure?
check.hint2: The first branch of unpack_result raises ToolFailure when is_error is true. It never reaches structured-content validation on that path.

It then forms the nested function definition used by DeepSeek. This is a deliberately narrow teaching adapter, not a universal schema converter. Local validation and permission checks remain in the executor after discovery.
review.worked_example: Function calling proposes the action; MCP carries the app-to-provider request. Comparing local and MCP routes should compare the actual offered definitions too: their descriptions or schema details may differ unless deliberately normalized.

We can now build and test the seminar wrapper before reconnecting DeepSeek.
review.worked_example: A resource can be present on a server while the model never receives it. A client-only resource test confirms retrieval, not a model explanation or an autonomous agent loop.

practice.title: Wrap the tested function instead of rewriting it
practice.logic: The server is an interface around a function we already trust enough to test. Its wrapper should not create a second source of specification data.
practice.explanation: MCPServer creates the server object. @server.tool registers the following function; it does not run it immediately. The return annotation dict[str, Any] and structured_output=True request structured output. The alias read_spec refers to the existing reader, avoiding an accidental call back to the wrapper itself. Known business failures become ToolError rather than successful-looking text. Use the lecture implementation to understand the pattern, then complete the seminar wrapper yourself.

practice.title: Structured results and honest failure signals
practice.logic: A string that looks like JSON is still text. A structured result lets the application inspect fields without guessing from a sentence.
practice.explanation: unpack_result first checks is_error. If it is true, the course raises a tool failure instead of treating the message as data. Next it requires a structured_content dictionary and validates our ToolResult envelope. status, data, source, version and error are this seminar's field names, not mandatory fields for every MCP server. The lecture uses an ok-based envelope, so do not interchange their keys.
practice.worked_example: Connection failure, unsupported protocol/schema, tool failure and an incorrect final model answer are different problems. A correct structured tool result is evidence to check the answer against, not a guarantee that the answer is correct.

check.explanation: unpack_result checks is_error before using data. An error message containing a number is not evidence of a successful tool result. Preserve the failure for diagnosis.
check.hint1: Which field tells the client whether the operation reported a failure?
check.hint2: The first branch of unpack_result raises ToolFailure when is_error is true. It never reaches structured-content validation on that path.

practice.title: Discovered metadata still needs an application decision
practice.logic: The model does not automatically see every tool advertised by a server. The host decides which definitions to offer and which requests to allow.
practice.explanation: adapt_spec_tool accepts only our expected specification tool and simple machine_id schema. It rejects unsupported schema shapes instead of silently dropping constraints. It then forms the nested function definition used by DeepSeek. This is a deliberately narrow teaching adapter, not a universal schema converter. Local validation and permission checks remain in the executor after discovery.

practice.title: Reading a resource does not put it in model context
practice.logic: A tool is invoked with arguments. A resource is content read through a resource interface. The difference is not simply whether data changes: our specification tool only reads.
practice.explanation: The lecture resource returns a short CONV-3 reference note. Reading that URI obtains content for the host. The host still has to select it and include it in a model request if it should affect the answer. That explicit selection is also why merely adding a resource is not a complete RAG system. We can now build and test the seminar wrapper before reconnecting DeepSeek.
practice.worked_example: A resource can be present on a server while the model never receives it. A client-only resource test confirms retrieval, not a model explanation or an autonomous agent loop.

check.prompt: The host reads the CONV-3 reference-note resource successfully, but sends DeepSeek only the original user question. Why can the model still lack the note?

options.A: Reading any resource automatically updates the model weights.

check.explanation: The resource response reaches the host. It is not automatically added to a model request. The host must decide what content belongs in that request; successful retrieval alone does not establish model context.
